evaluation.positioning_hook: A teenage girl trying to get off her pills is trapped in a night of escalating hauntings, as a black orb turns her friend group, family, and own mind against her.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The core promise is legible horror with a teen ensemble and a mental-health undercurrent, which gives it a clear audience lane. It’s more niche than broad because the script leans abstract and emotionally internal rather than delivering a clean monster or slasher engine.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The opening bathroom/pill imagery and the black figure establish unease quickly, but the central mechanism only really coheres once the orb and the repeated June 11 pattern emerge later. The premise is there, but it takes time to lock into a clean two-sentence pitch.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Sophia has a strong emotional center: she’s brittle, defensive, and visibly trying to survive both family pressure and something supernatural. The supporting friend group is vivid in fragments, but most of them are more atmosphere than fully differentiated engines.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script’s strongest move is the collision of teen intimacy, domestic dysfunction, and supernatural intrusion, with the pill-dropping and mirror imagery giving it a personal signature. It’s still working within familiar possession/haunting grammar, but the emotional framing is distinctive.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: There are effective jolts — the window figure, the lights failing, the electrocution, the blood splash — but the sequence is more episodic than escalating. The repeated resets and dreamlike transitions create mood, though they also soften forward drive.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The script has a fresh emotional hook in Sophia’s attempt to stop taking pills while a supernatural force seems to mirror her collapse. The idea is intriguing and personal, but the underlying haunting structure is still recognizable rather than truly singular.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The world has specific teen-social texture — school calendars, group chats, prom photos, field hockey, pacifist club, family custody paperwork — that makes the setting feel lived in. The supernatural rules are still impressionistic, so the world is richer in social detail than in mythic architecture.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The tone blends adolescent tenderness, domestic hostility, and uncanny dread in a way that feels emotionally specific. The script knows how to pivot from pillow fights and group hugs to foaming-mouth horror without losing its identity.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: The custody paperwork, the family tension, the repeated date of June 11, and the orb all suggest a deeper backstory beneath the surface scares. There’s a sense that the script is pointing to a larger emotional and supernatural logic even when it withholds explanation.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: The friend group has enough overlap to generate scenes — teasing, kissing, loyalty, jealousy, shared fear — and Sophia’s family adds a second pressure system. Still, the ensemble is more a cluster of reactions around Sophia than a fully self-propelling relationship machine.

lead_characters.name: Sophia
lead_characters.demographics: Teenage girl, likely high-school age; female; white/unspecified ethnicity; struggling with mental-health and family-custody pressure.
lead_characters.hook: Sophia is the script’s emotional and structural center: a guarded, exhausted teen who’s trying to hold herself together while her body, her home, and the supernatural world all seem to be turning on her. She’s defined by contradiction — affectionate with her friends, combative with her parents, and visibly ashamed of how fragile she feels — which makes her a strong vessel for both horror and empathy.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Kaitlyn Dever in Unbelievable or Elsie Fisher in Eighth Grade — a role built on raw interiority, defensive humor, and the kind of close-up vulnerability that can define a young actor’s career.

lead_characters.name: Jade
lead_characters.demographics: Teenage girl; female; friend of Sophia; emotionally close to Emma; likely high-school age.
lead_characters.hook: Jade reads as the most emotionally alert member of the friend group — playful, physically affectionate, and often the one who notices when the room shifts. She carries a quiet ache beneath the banter, especially in the scenes with Emma and in the later family reveal, which gives her more weight than a standard best-friend role.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Auli'i Cravalho in The Power or Rachel Sennott in Shiva Baby a chance to play warmth, panic, and subtext in the same scene — a supporting part with real emotional voltage.

lead_characters.name: Emma
lead_characters.demographics: Teenage girl; female; member of Sophia’s friend group; romantically linked to Bryan.
lead_characters.hook: Emma is one of the script’s most reactive presences: funny, physically present, and increasingly destabilized as the haunting intensifies. Her scenes with Jade and Bryan suggest a character who can carry both flirtation and fear, even if the page keeps her more impressionistic than fully defined.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of part that lets an actor do what Beanie Feldstein did in Booksmart or Odessa A'zion in Hellraiser — play comic ease first, then let the fear land harder because the audience already likes her.

lead_characters.name: Nancy
lead_characters.demographics: Teenage girl; female; friend in Sophia’s circle.
lead_characters.hook: Nancy functions as one of the group’s sharper observers, the person who spots the window disturbance and pushes the others to move. She’s not overexplained, but the script gives her enough presence to feel like a real member of the social ecosystem rather than a placeholder.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives a young actor a clean, scene-stealing utility part — think the grounded friend energy of a supporting turn in It or The Craft: Legacy, where a few precise beats can make the character memorable.

lead_characters.name: Maddy
lead_characters.demographics: Teenage girl; female; friend in Sophia’s circle.
lead_characters.hook: Maddy is quieter than some of the others but still gets a few telling beats, especially around the newspaper, the phone, and the emotional group scenes. She feels like one of the script’s texture characters — not central, but useful in making the friend group feel lived-in.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets an actor do subtle ensemble work in the vein of a supporting turn in The Perks of Being a Wallflower — present, specific, and emotionally readable without needing a monologue.

lead_characters.name: Sam
lead_characters.demographics: Teenage girl; female; friend in Sophia’s circle.
lead_characters.hook: Sam is part of the friend-group fabric and gets a few small but useful beats in the bedroom and hallway sequences. She reads as one of the people who makes the group feel like a real social unit, even when the script is moving fast.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of ensemble role that gives a young actor a foothold in a genre piece — the sort of part that can break out if the performer finds a strong, specific rhythm in limited screen time.

lead_characters.name: Phoebe
lead_characters.demographics: Teenage girl; female; friend in Sophia’s circle.
lead_characters.hook: Phoebe is mostly a presence in the group movement and transitions, but she helps widen the social field around Sophia. The script uses her as part of the collective energy that makes the haunting feel communal, not isolated.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a useful supporting ensemble slot for a young actor looking to enter the genre lane — not a fireworks role, but one with enough visibility to matter if the film lands.

lead_characters.name: Tina
lead_characters.demographics: Teenage girl; female; friend in Sophia’s circle.
lead_characters.hook: Tina gets one of the more memorable attitude beats when she confronts Bryan, which gives her a sharper edge than some of the other friends. She feels like a character with a little bite, even in a small footprint.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of scene that can give a supporting actor a quotable moment and a clear attitude, similar to the utility of a sharp teen role in a horror ensemble.

lead_characters.name: Bryan
lead_characters.demographics: Teenage boy; male; friend / romantic presence in the group.
lead_characters.hook: Bryan is one of the boys who shifts the social temperature in the group, moving between flirtation, teasing, and menace-adjacent behavior. He’s not deeply written, but he’s active enough to register as part of the relational friction around Sophia.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets a young actor play charm with a darker edge, similar to the kind of teen-boy part that can pop in a horror ensemble if the performer finds the right mix of swagger and unease.

lead_characters.name: Kyle
lead_characters.hook: Kyle is the closest thing the script has to a teen romantic anchor, but he’s also part of the social pressure around Sophia’s unraveling. He’s affectionate, casual, and slightly opportunistic, which makes him feel like more than a placeholder boyfriend.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that can give a young actor a clean romantic-supporting lane, with enough emotional ambiguity to avoid feeling like a stock boyfriend part.

lead_characters.name: Nate
lead_characters.demographics: Teenage boy; male; friend in the group.
lead_characters.hook: Nate is more of a missing-presence character than a fully active one, which is useful in a script that leans on absence and unanswered texts. His silence becomes part of the mystery texture.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a small but functional genre-supporting role — the kind of part that can matter if the actor gives the absence a distinct personality.

lead_characters.name: Tori
lead_characters.demographics: Adult woman, likely 30s-40s; female; Jade’s mother.
lead_characters.hook: Tori gives the script one of its clearest adult emotional counterpoints, moving from warmth to grief in the reveal around Jade’s father. She’s a good example of the script’s ability to make a supporting parent feel emotionally consequential in just a few scenes.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor a compact but potent emotional turn, similar to the parent roles that land in elevated genre films when they’re allowed to carry real grief.

lead_characters.name: Sophia’s Mom
lead_characters.demographics: Adult woman, likely 30s-40s; female; Sophia’s mother.
lead_characters.hook: Sophia’s mother is written as controlling, wounded, and volatile, with the custody paperwork and the lamp confrontation giving her real dramatic force. She’s not sympathetic in a simple way, but she’s not flat either — the script clearly wants her to feel like part of the pressure system around Sophia.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets an actor do hard, emotionally charged domestic conflict in the vein of a tense family-drama supporting turn — a part with real scene ownership if cast well.

lead_characters.name: Sophia’s Dad
lead_characters.demographics: Adult man, likely 30s-40s; male; Sophia’s father.
lead_characters.hook: Sophia’s father is quieter than the mother but still part of the family’s coercive atmosphere, especially in the custody and dinner-table scenes. He reads as exhausted, complicit, and emotionally underpowered, which gives the family dynamic a believable imbalance.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a strong supporting father role for an actor who can play restraint and moral fatigue — the kind of part that can feel bigger than the page if handled with specificity.

lead_characters.name: Sophia’s Sister
lead_characters.demographics: Child or young teen; female; Sophia’s younger sister.
lead_characters.hook: Sophia’s sister is a small but important emotional hinge in the family scenes, especially because she seems to sit inside the parents’ preferred version of the household. Her presence sharpens Sophia’s isolation without needing much dialogue.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of child supporting role that can be memorable through behavior alone — useful for a young performer who can communicate innocence and family allegiance without speeches.

lead_characters.name: Ruth
lead_characters.hook: Ruth is the emotional softener in the script, briefly restoring warmth and normalcy before the family and supernatural pressure reassert themselves. The dog also functions as a symbolic anchor for Sophia’s attempt to choose life and stability.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: For a production, this is the kind of animal role that can become a memorable emotional device if handled simply and cleanly.

locations.interior_exterior_ratio: mostly interior with some exterior day/night inserts
notable_requirements: suburban house with bedroom, bathroom, hallway, dining room, and exterior access

technical.vfx_details: primarily shadow movement, dark-figure appearances, flickering lights, and a few supernatural visibility effects; no large-scale digital build required on the page.
technical.sfx_needs: blood splatter, electrocution gag, foaming-mouth makeup, practical darkness/lighting effects, and orb/fire ritual practicals.

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model: streamer-first or specialty theatrical with a genre audience; the material is built for a contained, mood-forward horror launch.

budget.note: Contemporary house-based horror with a handful of exterior inserts, minor VFX, and practical scare work; the main cost pressure is night shooting rather than scale.

casting.note: Sophia has to carry grief, fear, dissociation, and teen volatility in the same role, and the friend group needs enough chemistry to make the ensemble feel real.

development.note: The orb, the repeated June 11 pattern, and the hospital-room coda suggest a larger mythology, but the script currently plays more like a mood-driven sequence than a fully legible feature engine.

comp_set.title: The Babadook
comp_set.why_it_comps: Like this script, it ties supernatural horror to grief, domestic pressure, and a protagonist whose inner state shapes the scare language.

audience_target.primary_audience: Teen and young-adult horror audiences who like emotional, character-forward supernatural stories with a strong female lead.
audience_target.demographics: Skews F18-34, with secondary pull for M18-34 and older horror fans who respond to grief-driven genre pieces.

budget_tier.note: Contemporary interiors, a small ensemble, practical effects, and limited VFX keep this in indie-feature territory, with night exteriors and a few specialty locations as the main scope drivers.

types_of_buyers: indie financiers looking for female-led genre material
lane_fit.detail: This sits naturally in the lane of emotionally charged, youth-skewing horror that can be sold on mood, performance, and a clean poster image. The friend-group structure and domestic pressure give it enough character texture for buyers who want genre with feeling, not just scares.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature; the supporting characters are vivid in the moment but do not yet suggest a separate franchise or spinoff vector.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Sophia is a strong horror lead.
strengths.what_it_means: The script gives a young actress a real showcase: emotional fragility, defensive attitude, and escalating terror all in one role. That is the kind of part that can attract casting attention from buyers looking for a breakout performance rather than a star vehicle.
strengths.evidence: The bathroom pill sequence, the confrontation with her mother, and the foaming-mouth collapse all put Sophia in sustained close-up crisis.

strengths.what_it_means: A horror film with a believable friend group is easier to market because the audience has a social world to attach to before the scares hit. That makes the project more attractive to buyers chasing youth-skewing genre with relationship texture.
strengths.evidence: The pillow-fight bedroom scene, the diner texting beat, and the amusement-park/pool sequences all build a recognizable group dynamic.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The domestic pressure is as scary as the haunting.
strengths.what_it_means: The family scenes add a second engine, which broadens the emotional appeal beyond pure supernatural horror. Buyers often respond to genre that can be sold on both external threat and internal pain, especially in the elevated lane.
strengths.evidence: The custody certificate, the lamp confrontation, and the parents’ cold treatment of Sophia create a hostile home environment that mirrors the supernatural dread.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The script has a clear visual motif system.
strengths.what_it_means: Recurring images like the mirror, the pills, the black figure, and the orb give the film a trailer-friendly identity. That kind of repeatable iconography helps a low-to-mid budget horror title punch above its weight in marketing.
strengths.evidence: The mirror/calendar hallway beat, the repeated bathroom pill imagery, and the final orb ritual all reinforce a coherent visual language.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The material is producible without a giant footprint.
strengths.what_it_means: A contemporary house-and-school horror film with limited VFX is a real advantage in the current market because it can be made economically and still feel premium. That makes it viable for indie financing, streamer acquisition, or a specialty theatrical path.
strengths.evidence: Most scenes live in bedrooms, hallways, bathrooms, a diner, and a few exterior day/night inserts, with the scares driven by practical effects and lighting.

whats_special.headline: This is a female-led, emotionally charged horror feature with a breakout central role, a believable teen ensemble, and a production footprint that stays inside indie economics. The combination of domestic dysfunction, supernatural dread, and strong visual motifs gives it a clean lane for streamer genre buyers and boutique horror financiers.

items.area: The orb mythology is still impressionistic.
items.detail: The black rusty object, the June 11 date, and the hospital-room voiceover hint at a larger system, but the feature currently plays more like a sequence of ominous events than a fully legible supernatural engine. That leaves buyers with a mood-forward package, but also a question about what the underlying rule set actually is.

After the initial haunting escalation, the script moves through school, amusement park, pool, diner, and family beats in a way that builds atmosphere more than forward momentum. A producer will notice that the scare pattern is effective moment to moment, but the feature spine is still loose.

items.area: Most supporting characters are texture, not engines.
items.detail: Jade, Emma, Nancy, Maddy, Sam, Phoebe, Tina, Bryan, Kyle, and Nate all help the social world feel real, but only a few of them have enough distinct desire or contradiction to drive scenes on their own. That limits relationship density and makes the film lean heavily on Sophia’s point of view.

items.area: The family conflict is potent but broad.
items.detail: The custody paperwork and the lamp confrontation give the home life real friction, but the parents are written in a fairly blunt register compared with the more specific teen material. That creates a slight tonal split between the nuanced friend-group scenes and the more generalized domestic antagonism.

issues.headline: The main friction is structural rather than tonal: the script has strong images and a compelling lead, but the supernatural logic is still hazy and the feature spine depends on a series of mood beats more than a clean engine. Buyers will also notice that the ensemble is effective as texture, yet most of the supporting cast is not yet built to carry much independent story weight.
